# Data

Structures and processes over data rather than over pixels: clustering and nearest-neighbour search, generative and constraint systems, graph dynamics, and the I/O helpers (files, JSON, subprocesses, OSC-adjacent devices) that get data into a box.

## FileManager.kt { #filemanager-kt }

Path resolution for the running Field session: turns a short spec into a real `File` or `Path`.
The `files` / `fileManager` properties (and the `String.file`, `String.path`,
`String.absolutePath` extensions) hand you the [`FieldFileManager`](data.md#filemanager-kt-fieldfilemanager) for the current box or
session, which resolves, in order: absolute and `~/` paths; `%document/…` and `%project/…`;
any name registered with `FileManager.add` or `FileManager["name"] = dir`; globs, by walking
the search roots and taking the first sorted match; and otherwise a plain relative name looked
up in the document's `files/` directory and then in the `files/` directory of every workspace
project the document belongs to.

Resolutions are cached per session and dropped when the named-directory table changes, and a
child path that would escape its root is rejected. Every lookup is appended to the session
root's `FILE_MANAGER_ACCESS_HISTORY_PROPERTY` property, trimmed to
`FileManager.maxAccessHistoryEntries` — so these calls need an active session or Box context and
will error without one.

## JSONLineServer.kt { #jsonlineserver-kt }

A TCP listener that turns newline-delimited JSON into a value a box can read each frame.
[`JSONLineServer`](data.md#jsonlineserver-kt-jsonlineserver) binds a `ServerSocket`, accepts any number of clients on daemon threads, and
keeps only the most recently received valid JSON line — `JSONLineServer.output` is a snapshot,
not a queue, so lines that arrive between reads are dropped. Non-JSON lines are counted in
`JSONLineServer.invalidLineCount` and logged, never thrown.

`jsonl` and [`JSONLineServers`](data.md#jsonlineserver-kt-jsonlineservers) hand out one cached, already-started server per
(port, bind host, backlog) so that re-running a box does not fight itself for the port;
ephemeral port 0 servers are rejected by the cache and must be built with `autoStart = false`.
Returning a [`JSONLineServer`](data.md#jsonlineserver-kt-jsonlineserver) from a box keeps it running for that box's run —
`registerJSONLineServerReturnValue` installs the `ReturnValueRegistry` handler that does it, and
an uncached server is stopped when the run ends.

## JSONProcess.kt { #jsonprocess-kt }

Runs an external command and reads newline-delimited JSON from its stdout. Build a
[`JSONProcess`](data.md#jsonprocess-kt-jsonprocess) with a working directory, a command and an optional environment; the most recent
parsable stdout line is exposed as `JSONProcess.output` (an `org.json.JSONObject`) — a snapshot
of the latest line, not a queue. A leading `~` is expanded in the working directory and in the
executable, but not in the remaining arguments.

Returning a [`JSONProcess`](data.md#jsonprocess-kt-jsonprocess) from a box starts the subprocess and ties it to that run:
`registerJSONProcessReturnValue` installs the `ReturnValueRegistry` handler, and the process is
destroyed — then force-destroyed if it will not exit — when the box re-runs or the job
completes. stdout and stderr are drained on daemon threads; non-JSON lines, stderr output and a
failure to start are recorded in `JSONProcess.lastError` and logged rather than thrown, so check
`JSONProcess.running`, `JSONProcess.exitCode` and `JSONProcess.hasOutput` to know what happened.

## SemanticSearchManager.kt { #semanticsearchmanager-kt }

Box-facing wrapper around `afield.ai.SemanticRetrievalService`, Field's embedding-based search
over source, docs and workspace boxes. Make a [`SemanticSearchManager`](data.md#semanticsearchmanager-kt-semanticsearchmanager) and call
`SemanticSearchManager.find` for the full [`SemanticSearchResult`](data.md#semanticsearchmanager-kt-semanticsearchresult) (message, status, hits) or
`SemanticSearchManager.findTopK` / `SemanticSearchManager.findWorkspaceTopK` when you just want
a `List<`[`SemanticSearchHit`](data.md#semanticsearchmanager-kt-semanticsearchhit)`>`; each hit carries score, kind, corpus, path and line range, and
prints as one readable line. Queries can be narrowed by corpus, path prefix, kind, document,
box or property, and note that `find` passes `rebuildIfEmpty = true` by default.

The remaining methods administer the service rather than query it:
`SemanticSearchManager.status`, `SemanticSearchManager.settings`, `SemanticSearchManager.enable`,
`SemanticSearchManager.saveSettings`, `SemanticSearchManager.downloadPreset`,
`SemanticSearchManager.rebuild`, `SemanticSearchManager.deleteIndex` and
`SemanticSearchManager.deleteModels`. Every call delegates straight through and blocks; the only
state kept here is `SemanticSearchManager.lastResult`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/SemanticSearchManager.kt`

## booleannetworks.kt { #booleannetworks-kt }

Synchronous Boolean networks and the pictures you draw of them. A [`BooleanNetwork`](data.md#booleannetworks-kt-booleannetwork) is a list of
[`BoolNode`](data.md#booleannetworks-kt-boolnode)s whose update lambdas all fire at once on the current state vector;
`BooleanNetwork.trajectory` and `BooleanNetwork.trajectoryUntilCycle` run one initial state
forward, and `BooleanNetwork.findAttractors` walks the whole `2^size` state-transition graph to
return every [`Attractor`](data.md#booleannetworks-kt-attractor) with its basin — it is `O(2^size)` and returns an empty list above 20
nodes.

The drawing helpers return `FLine`s for a box: `BooleanNetwork.drawUnrolled` (spacetime grid),
`BooleanNetwork.drawNetworkGraph` (wiring diagram on a circle),
`BooleanNetwork.drawStateTransitionGraph` (only for `size <= 6`),
`BooleanNetwork.drawAttractorBasins`, and the standalone `drawRhythmGrid` for any list of
Boolean lane states. `BooleanNetwork.notateHtml` and
`BooleanNetwork.notateAttractorsHtml` emit HTML tables instead, `BooleanNetwork.printAttractors`
plain text. Ready-made networks: `toggleNetwork`, `threeNodeNetwork`,
`segmentPolarityNetwork` and the random N-K `kauffmanNetwork`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/booleannetworks.kt`

**Used in:** [Boolean networks to FLine examples](../boolean_networks_examples.md), [Boolean network music examples](../boolean_network_music_examples.md)

### Top-level functions { #booleannetworks-kt-functions }

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">BooleanNetwork</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">trajectory</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">initial</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">BooleanArray</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">steps</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">BooleanArray</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code> | Advance `initial` forward by exactly `steps` synchronous updates. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">BooleanNetwork</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">trajectoryUntilCycle</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">initial</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">BooleanArray</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">maxSteps</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">1024</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">BooleanArray</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code> | Follow the trajectory from `initial` until a state repeats or `maxSteps` is exceeded. |

## clustering.kt { #clustering-kt }

Clustering for lists of `Float`, `Vec2`, `Vec3` and `Vec4`.

**There is no k-means here, on purpose.** Every algorithm in this file returns either a *hierarchy*
or a centre that is meaningful for the data it summarises: a medoid is one of your own samples, and
a median is coordinate-wise robust. A k-means centroid is neither, and on a point cloud with an
outlier it is the one that moves.

Hierarchical clustering — `floatAgglomerative`, `vec2Agglomerative`, `vec3Agglomerative`,
`vec4Agglomerative`, which wrap Smile's `HierarchicalClustering` over the seven
[`AgglomerativeLinkage`](data.md#clustering-kt-agglomerativelinkage)s — returns an [`AgglomerativeClustering`](data.md#clustering-kt-agglomerativeclustering) holding the merge tree, which you
cut into a [`ClusterLayer`](data.md#clustering-kt-clusterlayer) with `AgglomerativeClustering.partition`,
`AgglomerativeClustering.partitionByHeight` or `AgglomerativeClustering.layers`. The `…KMedoids`
and `…KMedians` functions are both local implementations in this file, each with D²-weighted
seeding and `KMedoidsOptions.runs`/`KMediansOptions.runs` restarts keeping the best objective:
k-medoids alternates assignment with an exact per-cluster re-medoid, k-medians is Lloyd's algorithm
on the L1 metric with a coordinate-wise median. Cuts of the merge tree come back with labels
renumbered by first appearance; every result type can be turned into a [`ClusterLayer`](data.md#clustering-kt-clusterlayer).

`visualizeVec3ClusterLayers3D`, `visualizeVec2ClusterLayers3D` and
`visualizeFloatClusterLayers3D` — plus the `AgglomerativeClustering.visualizeVec3`-style
extensions that build the layers for you — stack a list of [`ClusterLayer`](data.md#clustering-kt-clusterlayer)s along one axis and
return `FLine`s in a map keyed `"cluster-points"`, `"cluster-points-halo"`,
`"cluster-centers"`, `"cluster-centers-halo"`, `"cluster-links"` and `"cluster-guides"`.
[`ClusterLayerVizOptions`](data.md#clustering-kt-clusterlayervizoptions) controls spacing, sizes and which of those layers are emitted.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/clustering.kt`

**Used in:** [Points into structure — Voronoi, Apollonius, contours and clusters](../spatial_geometry_examples.md), [Typography as geometry — a string becomes contours](../typography_examples.md)

## dynamic_graph_field.kt { #dynamic-graph-field-kt }

The two honest ways to *look at* `dynamic_graph_systems.kt` — the point cloud and the weighted edges
joining it, so a time-varying graph can be watched rather than described.

It sits in its own file for the same reason `alife_field.kt` and `wfc_field.kt` do:
`dynamic_graph_systems.kt` names nothing from Field's visualizer or from the imaging family, and a
reader of it sees points, edges and clocks and nothing about pixels.

### Which of the two to use, because they are not interchangeable

| you want | call | why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a **figure** — one state, on a page, in a box | `dynamicGraphFLines` → `Box.showPlaneGrid` | vector: real `FLine`s through `drawToSVG`, so it scales, and edge weight drives colour *and* thickness |
| a **frame of an animation** | `dynamicGraphPanel` → `Box.animateEvolution` | raster: `Box.animateEvolution` encodes a `montage` of [`Img`](imaging.md#imaging-kt-img)s per frame, and there is no vector path into an mp4 |

`dynamicGraphFLines` is the default and `dynamicGraphImg`/`dynamicGraphPanel` are the animation
path. That split is deliberate and it is the whole reason this header exists: a hand-rolled
scan-converted pixel buffer is not how this codebase draws a figure — `FLine` →
`planeFigureHtml`/`drawToSVG` is — and the raster only survives here because
`Box.animateEvolution`'s `panels` lambda is typed `List<Pair<String, Img>>`
(`alife_animate.kt`), so a clip genuinely needs pixels. If you are reaching for
`dynamicGraphPanel` and you are not inside an `animateEvolution`, you want `dynamicGraphFLines`.

**The range policy, which is the whole difference between a picture and a lie.** Copied from
`alife_field.kt` because these are exactly the traps a graph animation walks into, and it applies
to both paths:

 - **The world window is the caller's, and it is fixed.** `dynamicGraphImg` takes an explicit
   `window`, and `Box.showPlaneGrid` takes one too, rather than fitting to the cloud: a cloud that
   is *moving* and *growing* re-fitted every frame appears to stand still while the world shrinks
   around it. `dynamicGraphWindow` computes a window once, from a reference state, for you to keep;
   `dynamicGraphPlaneWindow` converts it for the vector path.
 - **Edge weight is read against a `maxWeight` named by the caller**, not normalised per frame or
   per panel. Per-frame normalisation makes a graph that is uniformly saturating look identical to
   one that is uniformly dying, which is the single most misleading thing this family could draw.
 - **Points are drawn at the top of the ramp and edges below it**, so the population is legible even
   where the graph has decayed to nothing — an empty frame and a frame of isolated points are
   different states and must look different.
 - **A figure that clips says so.** `dynamicGraphImg` reports how many points fell outside the
   window in `DynamicGraphRaster.clipped` and `dynamicGraphOutsideWindow` answers the same question
   for the vector path, because a figure quietly cropping half its subject is the other way this
   goes wrong.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/dynamic_graph_field.kt`

**Used in:** [Graphs that change while you watch](../dynamic_graph_systems_examples.md)

## dynamic_graph_systems.kt { #dynamic-graph-systems-kt }

Time-varying point-and-edge systems: point clouds that move every frame while the graph joining
them is continually reinforced and decayed. State lives in [`DynamicPointState`](data.md#dynamic-graph-systems-kt-dynamicpointstate) (points, optional
`Vec4` labels, a clock), edges in [`DynamicEdgeList`](data.md#dynamic-graph-systems-kt-dynamicedgelist) (weight / age / ttl per edge, thinned by
`DynamicEdgeList.decayLinear` or `DynamicEdgeList.decayExponential`), and neighbour queries go
through [`Vec3SpatialHash`](data.md#dynamic-graph-systems-kt-vec3spatialhash), which is rebuilt each step because the cloud moves.

There are two extension points. A [`DynamicGraphSystem`](data.md#dynamic-graph-systems-kt-dynamicgraphsystem) only adds and reinforces edges —
[`Vec3BreathingAnisotropicKnnSystem`](data.md#dynamic-graph-systems-kt-vec3breathinganisotropicknnsystem), [`Vec3FlowlineAdvectionGraphSystem`](data.md#dynamic-graph-systems-kt-vec3flowlineadvectiongraphsystem),
[`Vec3LocalTangentTriangulationSystem`](data.md#dynamic-graph-systems-kt-vec3localtangenttriangulationsystem), [`Vec3PersistentProximityHysteresisSystem`](data.md#dynamic-graph-systems-kt-vec3persistentproximityhysteresissystem),
[`Vec3SignalRoutingGraphSystem`](data.md#dynamic-graph-systems-kt-vec3signalroutinggraphsystem), [`Vec3AlphaEventHypergraphCollapseSystem`](data.md#dynamic-graph-systems-kt-vec3alphaeventhypergraphcollapsesystem). A
[`DynamicPointProcess`](data.md#dynamic-graph-systems-kt-dynamicpointprocess) moves, adds and removes points against [`DynamicPointKinetics`](data.md#dynamic-graph-systems-kt-dynamicpointkinetics)
(velocity / resource / alive) and several are composed in order by [`DynamicProcessPipeline`](data.md#dynamic-graph-systems-kt-dynamicprocesspipeline).

Drive one frame with `stepDynamicGraph` or its decaying variants; `dynamicGraphSnapshot` and
`DynamicEdgeList.toPointGraph` convert the live edge store into the static `PointGraph` the rest
of the graph library expects, and `exampleDynamicMorphogenesisStep` wires a whole frame
together. Pure Kotlin, single-threaded, no external dependency.

**The population is not fixed, and three things have to agree about its size**: `state.points`,
[`DynamicPointKinetics`](data.md#dynamic-graph-systems-kt-dynamicpointkinetics) (via `DynamicPointKinetics.ensureSize`) and `DynamicEdgeList.pointCount`
(via `DynamicEdgeList.ensurePointCount` / `DynamicEdgeList.setPointCount`). `stepDynamicGraph`,
`DynamicProcessPipeline.step` and `exampleDynamicMorphogenesisStep` keep all three in step for
you; a hand-written [`DynamicPointProcess`](data.md#dynamic-graph-systems-kt-dynamicpointprocess) that appends a point *and* joins an edge to it in the
same call has to widen the store itself. See [`DynamicEdgeList`](data.md#dynamic-graph-systems-kt-dynamicedgelist) for what happens when it does not.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/dynamic_graph_systems.kt`

**Used in:** [Graphs that change while you watch](../dynamic_graph_systems_examples.md)

### MergeClosePointsProcess { #dynamic-graph-systems-kt-mergeclosepointsprocess }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">MergeClosePointsProcess</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">mergeDistance</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.025</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">minCombinedWeight</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">1.5</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">blend</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.5</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DynamicPointProcess</span></code>

Collapses pairs of points that are both within `mergeDistance` of each other *and* joined by an edge of at least `minCombinedWeight`: the higher-indexed one is absorbed into the lower, which takes the blended position, the blended velocity, the summed resource **and every edge the absorbed point had**.

## growing.kt { #growing-kt }

A 3-regular graph that grows by local rewriting. Every node in a [`GrowingGraph`](data.md#growing-kt-growinggraph) has exactly
three neighbours and one bit of state, and `GrowingGraph.grow` alternates two phases: compute
each node's next state and a "dividing" flag by indexing an integer rule with
`neighbour-count + 4 × state`, then apply a division to each flagged node that adds two nodes
and rewires their edges.

Seed the adjacency with `GrowingGraph.setNeighbors` (it must be a consistent 3-regular graph or
the rewrite throws), set states with `GrowingGraph.setState` or `GrowingGraph.randomizeStates`,
then call `grow()` per step and use the returned `GrowingGraph.GrowDelta` together with
`GrowingGraph.newEdgeU` / `GrowingGraph.newEdgeV` to draw only what changed. Storage is flat
`IntArray`/`ByteArray` with no per-node allocation and no allocation in the inner loops except
when capacity doubles; pure Kotlin, single-threaded, with a built-in xorshift64* generator for
the optional `flipProb` noise. `main` is a runnable 10-node demo.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/growing.kt`

### Top-level functions { #growing-kt-functions }

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">main</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span></code> | Small demo: start from K4 (tetrahedron), run a few steps, print size/state stats. |

### GrowingGraph { #growing-kt-growinggraph }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">GrowingGraph</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">initialNodeCount</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">rule</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">2182</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">flipProb</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">seed</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Long</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">1L</span><span class="p">)</span></code>

Self-contained Kotlin port of the "GrowingGraph" algorithm: - 3-regular graph: each node has exactly 3 neighbors - Binary state per node (0/1) - Two-phase grow(): Phase 0: compute next state + "dividing" flag from local neighborhood Phase 1: apply local rewrite (division) that adds 2 nodes and rewires edges

## jsonparsing.kt { #jsonparsing-kt }

Two related things: a small hand-written JSON reader, and a macro that generates a typed parser
from a terse schema. `parseJson` turns text into a [`JValue`](data.md#jsonparsing-kt-jvalue) tree — [`JObject`](data.md#jsonparsing-kt-jobject), [`JArray`](data.md#jsonparsing-kt-jarray),
[`JString`](data.md#jsonparsing-kt-jstring), [`JNumber`](data.md#jsonparsing-kt-jnumber) (which keeps the raw digits rather than converting), [`JBool`](data.md#jsonparsing-kt-jbool), [`JNull`](data.md#jsonparsing-kt-jnull) — and
throws [`JsonParseException`](data.md#jsonparsing-kt-jsonparseexception) with a character offset on bad input. No external JSON library is
involved.

`JsonSchemaGen.generateSource` compiles a schema such as `{name: s, at: [f, f], tags: `s...`,
...}` into Kotlin source for a data class with a `fromString` companion: `f`/`i`/`s` are the
leaves, ``x...`` is a list, `[a, b]` is a `Pair` (2, 3 or 4 floats collapse to `Vec2`/`Vec3`/
`Vec4`), and a trailing `...` permits extra JSON fields instead of rejecting them. In a box you
reach this through the `jsonParser<Name>("schema")` macro registered by
`registerJsonParsingMacros`, which inserts the generated source into the preamble. Inline nested
objects are not supported.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/jsonparsing.kt`

| Declaration | Summary |

| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">parseJson</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">src</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">JValue</span></code> | Parses JSON text into a [`JValue`](data.md#jsonparsing-kt-jvalue) tree. No external library, no reflection, no schema needed. |

### JValue { #jsonparsing-kt-jvalue }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">sealed</span> <span class="k">interface</span> <span class="nc">JValue</span></code>

A node of a parsed JSON document — one of [`JObject`](data.md#jsonparsing-kt-jobject), [`JArray`](data.md#jsonparsing-kt-jarray), [`JString`](data.md#jsonparsing-kt-jstring), [`JNumber`](data.md#jsonparsing-kt-jnumber), [`JBool`](data.md#jsonparsing-kt-jbool) or [`JNull`](data.md#jsonparsing-kt-jnull).

### JObject { #jsonparsing-kt-jobject }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">JObject</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">fields</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Map</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nc">JValue</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">JValue</span></code>

A JSON object. Field order is whatever the `Map` preserves, and a duplicate key keeps the last occurrence.

### JArray { #jsonparsing-kt-jarray }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">JArray</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">items</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">JValue</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">JValue</span></code>

A JSON array, in document order. Mixed element types are fine — each item is just a [`JValue`](data.md#jsonparsing-kt-jvalue).

### JString { #jsonparsing-kt-jstring }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">JString</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="k">value</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">JValue</span></code>

A JSON string, with escapes already decoded — so `value` is the real text, not the source form.

### JNumber { #jsonparsing-kt-jnumber }

A JSON number, kept as **the raw digits** rather than converted.

### JBool { #jsonparsing-kt-jbool }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">JBool</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="k">value</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">JValue</span></code>

A JSON `true` or `false`.

### JNull { #jsonparsing-kt-jnull }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">object</span> <span class="nc">JNull</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">JValue</span></code>

## numpy.kt { #numpy-kt }

Reader for NumPy's `.npy` and `.npz` on-disk formats. `npy` and `npz` are the short entry
points over [`NumpyIO`](data.md#numpy-kt-numpyio); `.npz` is unzipped into a `LinkedHashMap` of entry name to [`NpyArray`](data.md#numpy-kt-npyarray) and
must contain at least one `.npy` member. An [`NpyArray`](data.md#numpy-kt-npyarray) holds the raw payload bytes plus the
shape, the Fortran-order flag and an [`NpyDType`](data.md#numpy-kt-npydtype), and converts on demand via
`NpyArray.asDoubleArray`, `NpyArray.asFloatArray`, `NpyArray.asLongArray`,
`NpyArray.asULongArray`, `NpyArray.asBooleanArray` and `NpyArray.asComplexDoublePairs` —
Fortran-ordered data is remapped to C order unless you ask for `NpyLinearOrder.STORAGE`.

Read-only and pure JVM: there is no writer and no ndarray arithmetic. Format versions 1–3 are
accepted; bool, signed/unsigned int, half/float/double and complex64/128 decode, and any other
dtype kind (`NpyKind.OTHER`) throws. Element and byte counts must fit in an `Int`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/numpy.kt`

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">npy</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">path</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">NpyArray</span></code> | Reads a `.npy` file — `npy("data.npy").asDoubleArray()` is the whole idiom. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">npy</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">file</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">File</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">NpyArray</span></code> | Reads a `.npy` from a `File` — the overload to pair with `"data.npy".file`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">npz</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">path</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">LinkedHashMap</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nc">NpyArray</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code> | Reads a `.npz` archive into a map of member name to array, preserving the archive's own order. |

### NpyLinearOrder { #numpy-kt-npylinearorder }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">enum</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">NpyLinearOrder</span></code>

Which order to walk a multidimensional array in: `C` is row-major, last index varying fastest; `STORAGE` is however the file happens to hold it.

Constants: `C`, `STORAGE`.

### NpyByteOrder { #numpy-kt-npybyteorder }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">enum</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">NpyByteOrder</span></code>

The byte order a dtype declares, from the `<`, `>`, `=` or `|` character in its descriptor.

Constants: `LITTLE_ENDIAN`, `BIG_ENDIAN`, `NATIVE`, `NOT_APPLICABLE`.

### NpyKind { #numpy-kt-npykind }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">enum</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">NpyKind</span></code>

The family a dtype belongs to — what decides which conversion will accept it.

Constants: `BOOL`, `SIGNED_INT`, `UNSIGNED_INT`, `FLOAT`, `COMPLEX`, `OTHER`.

### NpyDType { #numpy-kt-npydtype }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">NpyDType</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">descriptor</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">byteOrder</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">NpyByteOrder</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">kind</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">NpyKind</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">itemSize</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">)</span></code>

## saved.kt { #saved-kt }

Per-box persistence for Kotlin values, on top of kotlinx.serialization. `var n by saved { 0 }`
declares a property that loads itself on first read and writes itself back on every assignment,
as JSON at `<document directory>/<box id>/<property name>.json`, encoded with Field's
`FieldJson` and written through the atomic `safeSave`. The no-argument `saved` overload skips
the default lambda but only for `List`, `Set` and `Map` (see `defaultSavedValue`); anything else
demands an explicit default.

The delegate itself is [`SavedJsonValue`](data.md#saved-kt-savedjsonvalue); it takes the box from its receiver or from the ambient
`Box.context`, so it needs an initialised box and session and errors out otherwise. `toJSONFile`
and `fromJSONFile` do the same encode/decode against an explicit `File` with no delegate. Any
failure to read, write or serialize is rethrown as a `SerializationException` naming the file.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/saved.kt`

## smile_neighbors.kt { #smile-neighbors-kt }

Nearest-neighbour indexes over `Vec2` / `Vec3` point lists, wrapping Smile's `KDTree` and `LSH`.
Build one with `vec2NN` or `vec3NN`: both copy the points, reject non-finite coordinates, and
return a [`Vec2NNIndex`](data.md#smile-neighbors-kt-vec2nnindex) / [`Vec3NNIndex`](data.md#smile-neighbors-kt-vec3nnindex) exposing `nearest`, `kNearest` and `withinRadius`. Results
come back as [`VecNeighbor2`](data.md#smile-neighbors-kt-vecneighbor2) / [`VecNeighbor3`](data.md#smile-neighbors-kt-vecneighbor3) carrying the index into the original list and the
true Euclidean distance, radius results sorted nearest-first.

`VecNNMode.APPROXIMATE` (the default) builds an LSH alongside the KD-tree and silently degrades
to exact mode, with a message on stderr, if LSH construction fails. The brute-force fallbacks are
narrower than they sound and do **not** make approximate mode correct: `kNearest` tops up an answer
that came back *short*, and `withinRadius` only runs one when the structure returns *nothing at all*,
so a full-length or merely-incomplete LSH answer is passed straight through. Ask for
`VecNNMode.EXACT` when the answer has to be right. [`VecNNBuildOptions`](data.md#smile-neighbors-kt-vecnnbuildoptions) tunes the LSH parameters and
can forbid duplicate points.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/smile_neighbors.kt`

**Used in:** [Neighbors & graph connectivity to FLine examples](../graph_connectivity_examples.md)

### VecNNMode { #smile-neighbors-kt-vecnnmode }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">enum</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">VecNNMode</span></code>

Which structure a [`Vec2NNIndex`](data.md#smile-neighbors-kt-vec2nnindex) / [`Vec3NNIndex`](data.md#smile-neighbors-kt-vec3nnindex) actually queries. `EXACT` searches the Smile KD-tree and returns the true nearest neighbours; `APPROXIMATE` (the default) searches a locality-sensitive hash instead, which only looks at points sharing a hash bucket with the query — so it can return the *wrong* neighbours, not merely take a different route to the right ones.

Constants: `APPROXIMATE`, `EXACT`.

class="p">.</span> <span class="o">&#42;</span><span class="p">/</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">allowDuplicatePoints</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">true</span><span class="p">)</span></code>

LSH build parameters and the duplicate-point policy for `vec2NN` / `vec3NN`. Only the approximate path reads the three `lsh` values; a `VecNNMode.EXACT` index ignores them entirely, so tuning them there changes nothing.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">lshBucketWidth</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Width of the LSH random projections, in the same units as your point coordinates. Wider buckets collect more points, so a query considers more candidates and is likelier to find the true neighbours, at more work per query; narrower buckets are cheaper and miss more. Must be finite and greater than zero. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">lshProjectionCount</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | How many random projections make up one LSH hash value. More projections mean more selective buckets, which is the same trade as a narrower `lshBucketWidth`: fewer candidates examined, more true neighbours missed. Must be greater than zero. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">lshUniversalHashSize</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | Size of the universal hash table behind each LSH hash; the default 9973 is prime. Bigger costs memory and reduces accidental collisions between unrelated buckets. Must be greater than zero. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">allowDuplicatePoints</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span></code> | Leave this true and duplicate points are indexed normally, simply showing up as several neighbours at the same distance. Set it false and `vec2NN` / `vec3NN` reject any list holding two bit-for-bit identical points, with an `IllegalArgumentException` naming the offending index. Note that this compares raw coordinate bits, so `0.0` and `-0.0` count as different points. |

One 2D neighbour hit: where the point sits in the list you built the index from, a copy of the point itself, and how far it is from the query. Handed back by [`Vec2NNIndex`](data.md#smile-neighbors-kt-vec2nnindex); there is no reason to construct one by hand.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">index</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | Position of this point in the list originally passed to `vec2NN`. The index takes a copy but preserves order, so this is safe to use as a key into your own parallel arrays. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">point</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Vec2</span></code> | A fresh copy of the indexed point, not the instance you passed in. `Vec2` is Field's mutable `Vector2f`, so writing to this cannot corrupt the index — and equally, mutating your original point after the build does not change what the index holds. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">distance</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | True Euclidean distance from the query to this point: not squared, and recomputed in `Double` from the stored coordinates rather than trusted from whatever the KD-tree or LSH reported. Zero when the query coincides with the point, which happens whenever you query with a point that is itself in the index. |

### Vec2NNIndex { #smile-neighbors-kt-vec2nnindex }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">Vec2NNIndex</span> <span class="k">internal</span> <span class="k">constructor</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">private</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">points</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Vec2</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">private</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">mode</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">VecNNMode</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">private</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">exactIndex</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">KDTree</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="o">?</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">private</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">approxIndex</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">LSH</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="o">?</span><span class="p">)</span></code>

A built 2D nearest-neighbour index — a private snapshot of the points plus the Smile structures that search them. Get one from `vec2NN` (the constructor is internal) and ask it for `nearest`, `kNearest` or `withinRadius`.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">size</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | How many points the index holds. This is the length of the snapshot taken at build time, so it never changes, and it is at least 1 because `vec2NN` rejects an empty list. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">nearest</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">query</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Vec2</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">VecNeighbor2</span></code> | The single closest indexed point to `query`, with its true Euclidean distance. Never null: the index is non-empty by construction, and if the backing structure declines to answer this falls through to a full scan. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">kNearest</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">query</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Vec2</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">k</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">VecNeighbor2</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code> | The `k` closest indexed points to `query`, with distinct indices and **no guaranteed order** — unlike `withinRadius` this never sorts, it returns candidates in whatever order the backing structure produced them, so sort by `distance` yourself if you need nearest-first. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">withinRadius</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">query</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Vec2</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">radius</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">VecNeighbor2</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code> | Every indexed point within `radius` of `query` — a true Euclidean distance, not a squared one — sorted nearest-first. Returns an empty list when nothing is in range; `radius` must be finite and at least zero or this throws. |

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">Vec3NNIndex</span> <span class="k">internal</span> <span class="k">constructor</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">private</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">points</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Vec3</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">private</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">mode</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">VecNNMode</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">private</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">exactIndex</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">KDTree</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="o">?</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">private</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">approxIndex</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">LSH</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="o">?</span><span class="p">)</span></code>

Never null: the index is non-empty by construction, and if the backing structure declines to answer this falls through to a full scan. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">kNearest</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">query</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Vec3</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">k</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">VecNeighbor3</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code> | The `k` closest indexed points to `query`, with distinct indices and **no guaranteed order** — unlike `withinRadius` this never sorts, it returns candidates in whatever order the backing structure produced them, so sort by `distance` yourself if you need nearest-first. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">withinRadius</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">query</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Vec3</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">radius</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">VecNeighbor3</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code> | Every indexed point within `radius` of `query` — a true Euclidean distance, not a squared one — sorted nearest-first. Returns an empty list when nothing is in range; `radius` must be finite and at least zero or this throws. |

## sorting_networks.kt { #sorting-networks-kt }

Sorting networks as data: a [`SortingNetwork`](data.md#sorting-networks-kt-sortingnetwork) is a wire count plus an ordered list of
[`SortingComparator`](data.md#sorting-networks-kt-sortingcomparator) compare-and-swaps. Build one with `SortingNetwork.bubble`,
`SortingNetwork.oddEvenMerge` (Batcher's iterative odd-even merge) or `SortingNetwork.anneal`
(simulated-annealing search for a shorter network), then check it with
`SortingNetwork.isSorting`, which enumerates all `2^n` binary inputs by the 0-1 principle up to
n = 20 and falls back to 4096 random probes above that.

`SortingNetwork.layers` assigns comparators to their earliest parallel layer (ASAP scheduling)
and drives `SortingNetwork.depth`, `SortingNetwork.notation` — a `"0:1 2:3 | 0:2 1:3"` string
that round-trips through `SortingNetwork.fromNotation` — `SortingNetwork.asciiDiagram` and
`SortingNetwork.toFLines` for `Box.lines(...)`. Pure Kotlin apart from `FLine`; the annealing
search is CPU-bound (each validity check is `O(2^n × |comparators|)`) and reports through
`afield.progressReporter`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/sorting_networks.kt`

**Used in:** [Sorting networks to FLine examples](../sorting_networks_examples.md)

## tuio.kt { #tuio-kt }

A minimal TUIO receiver. [`TuioReceiver`](data.md#tuio-kt-tuioreceiver) opens a UDP OSC port (3333 by default) through JavaOSC
and listens on `/tuio/2Dcur` and `/tuio/2Dobj` only — no blobs, no 2.5D or 3D profiles. It keeps
the live cursor and object sets, deduces additions and removals by diffing successive ALIVE
messages, and on each FSEQ message hands your [`TuioListener`](data.md#tuio-kt-tuiolistener) one `TuioReceiver.Frame` holding
both the full state and the per-frame added / updated / removed lists.

Call `TuioReceiver.start` to bind and `TuioReceiver.close` (or `stop()`) to release the port;
both are idempotent. Callbacks arrive on JavaOSC's receive thread, not yours, and all internal
state is guarded by one lock. Numeric OSC arguments are coerced leniently, and malformed `set`
messages are skipped rather than reported. `main` is a demo that prints frame deltas.

## wfc.kt { #wfc-kt }

Single-file, dependency-free Wave Function Collapse for Kotlin/JVM.

What this implements:
- Learns unique fixed-size tiles from a source PNG or 2D FloatArray.
- Learns adjacency constraints from a configurable symmetric neighborhood.
- Learns overlapping N x M patterns from a PNG or 2D FloatArray.
- Generates an output tile grid with an explicit step() loop for visualization.
- Avoids per-neighbor/per-tile garbage in propagation by using reusable LongArray bitsets.

Notes:
- The WFC solver operates only on integer tile IDs and constraints.
- PNG/FloatArray simple-tiled and overlapping helpers are intentionally separate from the core.
- The one concession to the rest of Field: [`WfcSolver`](data.md#wfc-kt-wfcsolver) implements [`afield.ToHTML`](visualization.md#valuevisualizer-kt-tohtml), so evaluating a
  solver in a box draws the collapse instead of a reflective property tree. Every pixel of that
  view lives in `wfc_field.kt` (`afield.stdlib.wfcSolverHtml`); this file names it once, in
  `WfcSolver.toHTML`, and depends on nothing else outside itself.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/wfc.kt`

**Used in:** [Wave Function Collapse examples](../wfc_examples.md)

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">WfcRulesBuilder</span> <span class="k">internal</span> <span class="k">constructor</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">tileCount</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">neighborhood</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">WfcNeighborhood</span><span class="p">)</span></code>

Weights bias both which tile a collapse picks and the entropy that decides *which cell* to collapse next; they default to `1.0` (uniform). |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">weights</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">vararg</span> <span class="n">values</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">)</span></code> | Set every tile weight at once, in tile-ID order. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">allow</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">direction</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">a</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">b</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">)</span></code> | Allow tile `b` to sit at `direction` from tile `a` — and, symmetrically, `a` at the opposite direction from `b`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">allow</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">dx</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">dy</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">a</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">b</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">)</span></code> | `allow`, addressing the direction by its offset instead of its index. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">allowAny</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">direction</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">a</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">vararg</span> <span class="n">others</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">)</span></code> | `allow(direction, a, b)` for every `b` in `others` — the common "a tolerates any of" case. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">allowMissingAnything</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span></code> | Fill in "anything goes" for every `(direction, tile)` pair still left empty, which is the defensive fallback `WfcRules.fromSampleGrid` applies to sample tiles it only ever saw at an edge. Off by default for hand-authored rules, because there an empty mask is more often a typo than an intention. |

## wfc_field.kt { #wfc-field-kt }

The bridge from Wave Function Collapse into the things Field already displays.

`wfc.kt` is deliberately dependency-free — it knows about integer tile IDs, `BufferedImage` and
`FloatArray`, and nothing else. That keeps the solver honest, but it means a box running WFC has
no direct way to *look* at what it is doing. These extensions supply the missing hop into
[`Img`](imaging.md#imaging-kt-img), and therefore into `Box.showImg`, `showImgGrid`, `montage`, `Img.colormap` and the
`ToHTML` thumbnail a box shows when you evaluate a value.

Three kinds of view:

 1. **The result.** `PngTileSet.toImg`, `PngOverlappingTileSet.toImg` and their `Float`
    counterparts turn a solved tile grid into an image. Pair them with
    `Img.upscaleNearest` — WFC output is pixels-as-pixels, and any filtering upscale destroys
    exactly the local structure you were trying to show.
 2. **The process.** `PngTileSet.waveToImg` renders a *partially collapsed* solver by blending
    each cell's still-possible tiles, and `WfcSolver.possibilityCountImg` exposes the
    possibility count per cell as a scalar field to colour-map. Sample either one inside a
    `while (solver.step() == WfcStatus.Running)` loop and you have the collapse itself as a
    sequence of frames — which is by far the most informative thing you can look at when rules
    are not behaving.
 3. **The solver, inline.** `wfcSolverHtml` is the body of [`WfcSolver`](data.md#wfc-kt-wfcsolver)'s own `ToHTML`, so simply
    *evaluating* a solver in a box — or `solver.h` — draws its current state: uncertainty,
    entropy, what has been decided, where it broke. Nothing to set up, no tile set needed. See
    `WfcSolver.possibilityCountHeatmapImg`, `WfcSolver.entropyHeatmapImg` and
    `WfcSolver.resolvedTileImg` for the three panels on their own.

Because a solved cell has exactly one possibility, `waveToImg` on a `WfcStatus.Solved` solver is
the finished output: the animation's last frame and the result are the same picture, by
construction rather than by coincidence.
